title: Your paginated list collapses at page 500 — how do you fix it?
description: Why OFFSET pagination degrades, keyset/cursor pagination mechanics, and how to support jumping to arbitrary pages.

data.text: OFFSET-based pagination looks innocent at page 1 and collapses at page 500: the database must generate and discard every preceding row before returning your 20 — OFFSET 9980 means scanning 10,000 rows to skip them. Latency grows linearly with depth, indexes can't avoid the skip, and rows shifting between pages (new inserts, deletes) cause items to be skipped or repeated. Deep offsets also let an attacker or scraper walk your entire table with simple requests.

The interviewer is testing whether you know the difference between positional and value-based navigation, and whether you understand that 'infinite scroll' and 'jump to page 97' are different products with different database costs. Keyset pagination is the fix for sequential navigation; arbitrary page jumps need a deliberate, bounded alternative.

**OFFSET/FETCH (positional):**
- `ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC OFFSET 9980 FETCH NEXT 20` — the engine sorts (or walks the index), then throws away 9,980 rows
- Cost is O(offset): every page is more expensive than the last
- Consistency: rows inserted/deleted between requests shift the window → duplicates and skips
- Only viable when 'jump to arbitrary page' is a real requirement AND depth is bounded

**Keyset/cursor (value-based):**
- Page by value: `WHERE (CreatedAt, Id) < (@lastCreatedAt, @lastId) ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC, Id DESC` — the index seeks straight to the next row
- Cost is O(page size) regardless of depth — page 5,000 costs what page 1 costs
- Stable under concurrent writes: the cursor anchors on a value, not a position
- The cursor is an opaque token (encode last key values, sign it if clients could tamper)
- Requires a **total order**: add a unique tiebreaker (`Id`) or you'll skip ties on duplicate CreatedAt
- Cursor must change when sort/filter changes — key it by query shape (or hash the sort into the token)
Code: keyset pagination with a composite cursor

data.title: SQL Server: seek, don't skip
data.code:
-- First page
SELECT TOP (20) Id, CreatedAt, Title
FROM Orders
ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC, Id DESC;

-- Subsequent pages: seek directly to where the last page ended.
-- (CreatedAt, Id) is a total order thanks to the Id tiebreaker.
SELECT TOP (20) Id, CreatedAt, Title
FROM Orders
WHERE (CreatedAt, Id) < (@prevCreatedAt, @prevId)   -- seek predicate
ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC, Id DESC;

-- Index that makes the seek possible:
CREATE INDEX IX_Orders_CreatedAt_Id
ON Orders (CreatedAt DESC, Id DESC)
INCLUDE (Title);

-- ❌ What we're replacing:
-- SELECT ... ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC
-- OFFSET 9980 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY;  -- scans & discards 9,980 rows

-- Filtering + keyset: keep the filter in every page, cursor only handles position
-- WHERE Status = @status AND (CreatedAt, Id) < (@prevCreatedAt, @prevId)

data.title: Minimal API: opaque cursor round-trip
Keyset needs a total order
data.text: Ordering by a non-unique column alone (CreatedAt) silently skips or repeats rows when values tie. Always append a unique tiebreaker such as Id to both the ORDER BY and the seek predicate — and mirror it in the index.

items: Keyset cannot answer 'jump to page N' directly — products must decide if that feature is worth the cost.
Cursor leaks: sign it (HMAC) or validate structure so clients can't forge predicates.
Sort changes are cursor changes: 'sort by amount' must mint a new cursor family.
Counts: '10,432 results' stays expensive either way — approximate counts, cache them, or drop exactness.
Infinite scroll + keyset is the natural pairing; OFFSET keeps a role for bounded admin tables.
The same logic applies to GraphQL Relay-style connections (edges + pageInfo.endCursor) — the pattern is universal.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: OFFSET cost grows with depth; keyset seeks straight to the next row.
Composite cursor (value, Id) + matching index = O(page size) at any depth.
Keyset is stable under concurrent writes; OFFSET shifts rows between pages.
Bound page sizes, sign cursors, and keep arbitrary page jumps on a bounded OFFSET path.
data.takeaway: Paginate by value, not by position: a seek predicate on an indexed total order keeps page 5,000 as cheap as page 1.
